title: A new commandment (John 13:31–38)
hook: love one another as I have loved you; by this all will know

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beloved disciple leaning close, and Judas taking the bread and going out. Your line was and it was night.

Why is the Thursday before Easter called Maundy Thursday? Maundy is an odd word; outside this one week, English hardly uses it. It comes from Latin. In the old Latin Bible, today's verse begins with the words mandatum novum, a new commandment. Mandatum became maundy. So a whole day of the Christian year is named after one sentence Jesus spoke at supper, right after Judas walked out into the night. The room is quieter now. And Jesus speaks to the eleven who are left, like a father at the end.

He calls them little children, the only time in John's Gospel he does, and tells them he's going where they can't follow yet. Then: "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another." Love one another isn't new on its own. The law of Moses already says, love thy neighbor as thyself, and Jesus himself quoted it. So what's new? The measure: not as you love yourself, but as I have loved you. They've just seen it: a towel, a basin, and feet, including the feet of the one who left. Then the sign: "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." Not by a badge, a building, or a set of correct opinions. By love they can see. Around the year two hundred, a Christian writer in North Africa named Tertullian reported what outsiders said of the Christians they knew: see how they love one another. Then Peter interrupts: why can't I follow you now? "I will lay down my life for thy sake." He means it. And Jesus answers with sad honesty: "The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice." Even the friend who promises the most will fail tonight. The new commandment is given to people who will need it. Look back over this week: a frightened council, nard filling a house, a grain of wheat, walking in the light, a towel and basin, a disciple leaning close, and now love as the sign.
screen: `PETER: I WILL LAY DOWN MY LIFE.`
then, large: `AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose love for you has been visible, not just felt but seen, and what they did. Then think of someone you love, maybe not visibly enough, and picture one thing they would actually see: a note, a meal, an hour, showing up. If you pray, ask to love as you've been loved; if not, simply decide on the one thing.
Tertullian. A Christian writer in North Africa who reported what outsiders said of believers: see how they love one another.
Your line: by this, all will know. Love they can see. Day six hundred thirty, and a week well walked.

howItsDone: Christians remember the new commandment on Maundy Thursday, often with footwashing, communion and the stripping of the altar; many churches also take it as the measure of their common life.

chat.says: Love your neighbor was already old. So what's new about Jesus's new commandment?
options: The measure: love one another as I have loved you, like washing their feet.
The new part is loving God, since the old law spoke only of neighbors.
The new part is that love is a feeling now, not something you show.
chat.meaning: Love one another was already in the law of Moses. What's new is the measure: as I have loved you. A towel, a basin, and feet.

Maundy Thursday.meaning: the Thursday before Easter, named for the new commandment

law of Moses.meaning: the old law that already said, love thy neighbor

Tertullian.meaning: a Christian writer in North Africa around the year two hundred

sources.quoted: A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another.
By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
I will lay down my life for thy sake.
The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice.

notes: 'Little children' (teknia, 13:33): the only time in John's Gospel Jesus uses this word (1 John uses it often). Confirm.
'Love thy neighbor as thyself' is close to KJV Leviticus 19:18 ('thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself'); paraphrased with American spelling, not marked as quotation. Confirm.
Etymology Maundy < Latin mandatum (Vulgate John 13:34, 'Mandatum novum do vobis'): standard. Confirm.
Tertullian, Apology 39 (c. AD 197): 'see how they love one another' paraphrased. Confirm.

Audit (y2 10% sample): 'nobody uses it anywhere else' was untrue (e.g. Britain's Royal Maundy, itself a Maundy Thursday custom); softened. 'The one who loves him most' was an unsourced ranking of the disciples; changed to 'the friend who promises the most'.
